concepts.name: Fill and empty rates
concepts.description: A pipe that fills a tank in n hours adds 1/n of it per hour; an outlet removes 1/n per hour.

concepts.name: Pipes working together
concepts.description: Add the rates of inlets, subtract the rates of outlets, then invert.

concepts.name: Leaks
concepts.description: A leak is just an outlet you did not ask for: compare fill times with and without it.

concepts.name: Changing the setup part-way
concepts.description: Work out the fraction done first, then the rate for the remaining stage.

formulas.title: Pipe rate
formulas.prompt: A pipe fills a tank in n hours. What fraction does it fill per hour?
formulas.explanation: Same idea as work rates: convert time into a fraction per hour so that rates can be added.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A pipe fills a tank in 12 hours. What fraction of the tank does it fill in one hour?

formulas.title: Net rate
formulas.prompt: With several pipes open, how do you find the time to fill?
formulas.formula:
Net rate = (sum of inlet rates) − (sum of outlet rates)
Time = 1 ÷ Net rate
formulas.explanation: Inlets add water, outlets remove it. A positive net rate fills the tank; a negative one empties it.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the outlet's rate instead of subtracting it.
formulas.applicationPrompt: An inlet fills a tank in 4 hours and an outlet empties it in 12. With both open, how long to fill?

formulas.title: The leak
formulas.prompt: A tank fills in a hours normally but takes b hours with a leak (b > a). How long does the leak take to empty a full tank?
formulas.formula:
Leak rate = 1/a − 1/b
Emptying time = ab ÷ (b − a)
formulas.explanation: The leak's rate is the difference between the rate without it and the rate with it.
formulas.applicationPrompt: A tank normally fills in 5 hours but takes 6 with a leak. How long would the leak take to empty it?

formulas.title: Staged problems
formulas.prompt: A setup changes part-way. How do you find the total time?
formulas.formula:
Fraction done = rate₁ × t₁
Remaining ÷ rate₂ = t₂
formulas.explanation: Treat each stage as its own problem with the whole tank as 1.
formulas.example:
Rate 1/6 for 4 hr → 2/3 done
Remaining 1/3 at 1/15 → 5 hr
formulas.commonMistake: Using the first rate for the whole job.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Two pipes fill in 10 and 15 hours. Both open for 4 hours, then the first is closed. How many more hours does the second need?

formulas.title: Tank capacity as the LCM
formulas.prompt: How do you combine filling and emptying pipes without fractions?
formulas.formula:
Capacity = LCM of the times
Inlet: + Capacity ÷ time   Outlet: − Capacity ÷ time
Time = Capacity ÷ net units per minute
formulas.explanation: With the LCM as the capacity, every pipe moves a whole number of units per minute.
formulas.example: Pipes fill in 20 and 30 minutes, an outlet empties in 15: capacity 60, net 3 + 2 − 4 = 1 a minute, so 60 minutes.
formulas.commonMistake: Adding the outlet's units instead of subtracting them.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Two inlets take 12 and 15 hours; a drain empties the tank in 20 hours. All are open.

formulas.title: When to close the second pipe
formulas.prompt: Pipes A and B fill a tank in a and b minutes. Both are opened; when must B be closed for the tank to fill in exactly T minutes?
formulas.formula: Close B after b × (1 − T/a) minutes
formulas.explanation: A runs for all T minutes and fills T/a of the tank; B only has to supply the rest.
formulas.example: a = 24, b = 32, T = 18: close B after 32 × (1 − 18/24) = 8 minutes.
formulas.commonMistake: Giving B the full T minutes as well.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Pipes fill in 12 and 16 minutes. Both start; the tank must be full in exactly 9 minutes.

levels.title: A Tank Is a Job
levels.description: Pipes are workers: inlets add, outlets subtract.

blocks.title: Same as time and work
blocks.body: A pipe that fills a tank in 12 hours fills 1/12 of it every hour. An outlet that empties it in 12 hours removes 1/12 every hour. Because they are rates, you can add and subtract them — you can never add the times.

blocks.title: Net rate
blocks.caption: A positive net rate fills the tank; a negative one drains it.

blocks.title: Outlets slow you down
blocks.body: With an inlet of 1/4 and an outlet of 1/12, the tank gains 1/6 per hour, so it fills in 6 hours — longer than the inlet alone would take.

levels.title: Pipes Formulas
levels.description: Rates, net rates, leaks and staged problems.

levels.title: Leaks, Missing Pipes and Part-Full Tanks
levels.description: Subtracting rates to find the unknown.

questions.question: A pipe fills a tank in 12 hours. What fraction of the tank does it fill in one hour?
questions.explanation: Twelve equal hours fill the whole tank, so one hour fills 1/12.
solutionSteps: It is filled evenly over 12 hours.

hints.text: If the whole tank is 1, how much does one hour add?

questions.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and pipe B fills it in 3 hours. How many hours will they take to fill it together?
questions.explanation: 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 1/2 per hour, so together they take 2 hours.

hints.text: Convert each time into a rate.
Use 6 as the common denominator.

questions.question: An inlet fills a tank in 4 hours and an outlet empties it in 12 hours. If both are open, how long does it take to fill the empty tank?
questions.explanation: Net rate = 1/4 − 1/12 = 3/12 − 1/12 = 2/12 = 1/6, so the tank fills in 6 hours.

hints.text: An outlet works against the inlet.
Subtract 1/12 from 1/4.

commonMistakes: Adding the rates (3 hours), averaging the times (8), or adding the times (16).

questions.question: An inlet fills a tank in a hours and an outlet empties it in b hours (b > a). With both open, the fraction filled per hour is
questions.explanation: The inlet adds 1/a per hour and the outlet removes 1/b, so the net is 1/a − 1/b. It is positive because b > a means the outlet is slower.

hints.text: Does the outlet add water or remove it?

questions.question: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 20 and 30 minutes. A third pipe C can empty the full tank in 15 minutes. If all three are opened together, how many minutes does it take to fill the empty tank?

hints.text: Convert each pipe into a rate over 60.
C works against A and B.

questions.question: A pipe fills a tank in 5 hours. Because of a leak, it takes 6 hours to fill. How long would the leak alone take to empty the full tank?
questions.explanation: Leak rate = 1/5 − 1/6 = 6/30 − 5/30 = 1/30, so it empties a full tank in 30 hours.
questions.method: Leak rate = normal rate − actual rate.

hints.text: The extra hour is not the emptying time.
Subtract the two rates.

commonMistakes: Answering the extra hour (1) or adding 5 + 6 (11).

questions.question: Pipe A alone fills a tank in 15 minutes. A and B together fill it in 10 minutes. How many minutes would B alone take?
questions.explanation: B's rate = 1/10 − 1/15 = 3/30 − 2/30 = 1/30, so B alone takes 30 minutes.
questions.method: Subtract rates to isolate the missing pipe.

hints.text: Rates subtract as well as add.
Invert B's rate.

commonMistakes: Subtracting the times (10 − 15 → negative) or getting 5.

questions.question: A tank is half full. A pipe can fill a full tank in 8 hours and a waste pipe can empty a full tank in 24 hours. With both open, how long does it take to fill the rest of the tank?
questions.explanation: Net rate = 1/8 − 1/24 = 3/24 − 1/24 = 1/12 per hour. Only half a tank remains, so 1/2 ÷ 1/12 = 6 hours.

hints.text: How much of the tank still needs filling?
Do not use a full tank in your calculation.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the tank is half full (12 hours).

questions.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 10 hours and pipe B in 15 hours. Both are opened together, and after 4 hours A is closed. How many more hours does B need to fill the rest of the tank?
questions.explanation: Together: 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6 per hour, so in 4 hours they fill 4/6 = 2/3. The remaining 1/3 at B's rate of 1/15 takes 5 hours.
questions.method: Stage 1: rate × time. Stage 2: remaining ÷ new rate.

hints.text: First find how much is filled in the first 4 hours.
Then only B is working.

commonMistakes: Using B's rate for the first stage too.

questions.question: Pipes A and B can fill a tank in 12 and 15 minutes, and a pipe C can empty it in 20 minutes. All three are opened together; after 4 minutes C is closed. In how many minutes from the start is the tank full?
questions.explanation: Call the tank 60 units: A adds 5, B adds 4, C removes 3 per minute. With all open the net is 6 per minute, so 4 minutes give 24 units. Then C is closed: 9 per minute for the remaining 36 units takes 4 minutes. Total = 8 minutes.
solutionSteps: Tank = 60 units; A = 5, B = 4, C = −3 per minute.
questions.method: Use the LCM as the tank size and run the stages one after another.

hints.text: Pick 60 units as the capacity so every pipe has a whole rate.
Find the net rate for each stage separately.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to include the first 4 minutes in the total.

questions.question: A pipe fills 3/8 of an empty tank in 6 hours. At the same rate, how long does it take to fill the whole tank?
questions.explanation: The pipe fills 3/8 of the tank in 6 hours, so 1/8 takes 6 ÷ 3 = 2 hours. The whole tank is 8 eighths: 8 × 2 = 16 hours.
questions.method: Time for the whole = time for the part ÷ fraction filled.

hints.text: How long does 1/8 of the tank take?
A full tank is 8/8.

commonMistakes: Multiplying 6 by 3/8 instead of dividing (2.25 hours).
Multiplying 6 by 8 and forgetting the 3 (48 hours).

questions.question: A full tank has a leak that can empty it in 8 hours. If an inlet pipe that adds 6 litres per minute is also kept open, the full tank empties in 12 hours. What is the capacity of the tank, in litres?
questions.explanation: Let the capacity be C litres. The leak alone removes C/8 litres an hour. The inlet adds 6 × 60 = 360 litres an hour. With both open the full tank empties in 12 hours, so C/8 − 360 = C/12. Then C/8 − C/12 = C/24 = 360, giving C = 8640 litres.
solutionSteps: Leak: C/8 litres/hour; net emptying with both: C/12 litres/hour.
questions.method: Leak rate − inlet rate = net emptying rate; the gap between the two fractions equals the inlet's litres per hour.

hints.text: Change 6 litres a minute into litres an hour.
Write the leak's hourly rate and the net hourly rate as fractions of C.
The difference between those two rates is exactly what the inlet supplies.

commonMistakes: Adding the inlet to the leak instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: Pipes A and B can fill an empty tank in 6 hours and 9 hours respectively. They are opened alternately for one hour each, starting with A, and only one pipe is open at a time. How long does it take to fill the tank?
questions.explanation: In each 2-hour cycle A then B fill 1/6 + 1/9 = 5/18 of the tank. After 3 cycles (6 hours) 15/18 is full and 3/18 = 1/6 remains. It is A's turn, and A fills exactly 1/6 in the next hour. Total = 7 hours.
solutionSteps: One cycle (A for 1 hour, then B for 1 hour) fills 1/6 + 1/9 = 5/18.
A works in hour 7 and fills 1/6 exactly.
questions.method: Fill cycle by cycle, then finish the last part with whichever pipe is on duty.

hints.text: How much do A and B fill in one 2-hour cycle?
Stop the whole cycles before the tank would overflow.
Whose turn is it when the last part is left?

commonMistakes: Letting B take the first hour (7 hours 20 minutes).
